Author, per the Draft Forum's new policy: http://www.scp-wiki.net/forum/t-10629348/new-draft-forum-policies authors who have not yet posted a successful mainsite article are now required to get their basic concept(s) greenlighted by two experienced reviewers in the Ideas Critique forum and/or IRC chatrooms before asking for draft feedback.

Please first go to the Ideas forum or the chat, give a quick summary (for the Ideas forum, please follow the instructions in the required reading thread) of the concept you want to write up (don't link the draft unless someone requests it), and reviewers can help you make sure that your core idea is something that will be successful with the community audience.

During the conceptualization stage, reviewers can also help by letting you know if something similar already exists on the site, and/or telling you if there are any cliches/pitfalls/other typical downvote reasons to be careful of with your particular idea. These issues are more effectively addressed earlier on in the writing process.

If you have already received the requisite greenlights, please note from whom and where you received them. If you would like to receive draft critique without going through the greenlighting process, please use the IRC chatrooms to request reviews.

item.title: Re: The Nanny
item.content:encoded:
Hey! Appreciate the DM reminder. Apologies for making you wait. I get wrapped up in other things and forget to check back in ‘round here.

Okay, so, you have a decent set-up here. It’s a little 2011 but there’s nothing wrong with that. But I do think what you have is only a basic starter for a robust SCP article and it’s pretty close to SCP-610.

I want to know more about these characters. I need you to bring them to life for me because what you have here are cardboard cut-outs. You have a decent creepy idea but you need to a) flesh it out into a full-fledged story, and b) differentiate it from SCP-610 a little more. And I think the characters are where you can accomplish that.

I can’t give you a greenlight but I want you to marinate on the world you’re creating until someone else else does. Your big hurdle here is figuring out the story you want to tell with the framework you’ve created. Don’t be afraid to reach out to an experienced author if your idea goes another few days without further comment.

Godspeed, homie. ✌️

item.title: Re: Help: Addendum usage?
item.content:encoded:
For example its creators, where the Foundation found it, what attracted the Foundation to it, etc. Would that go in addendum or somewhere else like a log sort of?

Depends on how key the backstory is to understanding the basic anomaly. If it's difficult to understand the absolute basics of what the anomaly does without the backstory, put the backstory in the description.

One definition of "addendum" is "an item of additional material, typically omissions, added at the end of a book or other publication." Addenda are additions to the primary description content. Since Foundation discovery tends to not be crucial to basic description of an anomaly, that content usually is put in addenda.

So far as logs go, it depends on the content in said logs. I typically encourage logs only if the format is conducive to storytelling; if you have information that is well-presented in a short paragraph, there's no need to have an entire drawn-out log just for the sake of a log.

item.title: The Macguffin
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch: An old locket, when someone touches it they begin on a journey to face some evil person or organization. They’ll defeat the villain in some epic showdown and everyone lives happily ever after.

+ Yay! Happily ever after!
- Yeah, of course there’s more

There’s a few catches. First, someone always touches the locket, it’s destiny. That’s not to say that this is uncontainable, but the journeys need to be managed instead of prevented. Which is especially difficult due to catch two, the Foundation meets all the requirements to be a villain. So their top priority is obviously making sure they never get selected as a target. But then comes in catch three, because the obvious containment method is to simply send someone on a scripted adventure. But when you script the adventure, you become the villain. I don’t know if you’ve caught on by now but this article is all about the Foundation trying to contain fate, which is completely illogical. But the thing is, they do it.

Central Narrative: The meat of the story will be told through test logs where the Foundation will experiment with different containment procedures. For instance, what happens if you have someone touch the locket, then you terminate them? (Spoiler alert, the same thing that happens when the protagonist of a book is facing down a firing squad, it doesn’t end well for the firing squad). In the end, they contain it by having an independent task force act as the villains. The task force doesn’t know they’re meant to be villains, they know that they have one objective, “kill anyone who touches the locket”. They also know that they keep failing. Since the task force isn’t directly controlled by the Foundation, the Foundation is safe from becoming the villains.

Hook/Attention-Grabber: Two things. One, fate isn’t that common of a system to show up in SCPs. The second one I haven’t mentioned yet, but this is actually a completely non lethal SCP. The person affected by the locket is both incapable of dying and incapable of killing people. That’s not to say it’s not dangerous though. I’m considering adding a discovery log where someone with this locket collapses a corporation that was exploiting people, but at the same time puts millions of people out of work.

Additional Notes: I want to know if you think this is too many ideas in one or if it ties together well.

item.title: Re: The Friendly Shadow
item.content:encoded:
Got a PM about this, took a quick look. I'll admit that I'm not super enthusiastic about the concept—but a lot of my response is likely due to personal preference, seeing as two greenlights have already been given.

To start, remember the difference between sapient and sentient. Dogs and cats and sometimes lobsters are considered sentient—for human-level intelligence and self-awareness, you'd want sapience.

+ show block
– hide block

My main issue with the concept is that to me Tom doesn't really seem like a believable origin point for Clarence. There's no mention of 3-D human Clarence having any difficulty navigating a world that is fundamentally different from Tom's. I as a reader am a bit skeptical about the Foundation finding out that Tom "created" Clarence when they were children (was Clarence adopted? Did no one notice that he had a shadow that would interact with him, all throughout his childhood, adolescence, and presumably young adulthood??) and is able to lie to him via charades. I'm also unsure of how the Foundation would be able to find out that Tom has a "shadow world" of his own that he was originally from.

I guess in general I'm just very skeptical about how well the story would hold up with the "shadow world" explanation. There are a lot of things that happen to shadows that don't happen to people: shadows can become warped or distorted or multiplied depending on the intensity and positioning of the light on the item that casts the shadow, larger shadows envelop smaller shadows, and so on. If these are experiences inherent to Tom, why doesn't Clarence seem confused that he has a different experience? Also, if Tom has his own shadow world where he's 3-D, why did he manifest into the world that humans live in? It also seems unusually convenient that the guy just happens to get kicked out of his original world but also just happens to be able to manifest a "shadow" that works in the world of humans. Also seems odd that Tom/Clarence just happen to be human—if Tom comes from an otherworldly place and needs the means to navigate the world quickly, why use a human as opposed to something more maneuverable? Or does Tom just happen to get lonely too, necessitating Clarence?

I guess in general I'm just confused about Tom's motivations and what he is beyond just "sapient shadow like Peter Pan's". It shouldn't be too difficult to tweak the setup though. My suggestions:

  • have both Tom and Clarence slip up a few times. Clarence sometimes tries to tilt objects towards other objects to reach things instead of stretching his own body, because he forgets that he can't stretch the way shadows/Tom can. Tom doesn't understand how certain items break when dropped (since in the case of, say, a mirror that has a crack in it, the shadow shape remains the same)
  • have Tom and Clarence use their own form of modified sign language (can't just be ASL since some handshapes/signs look identical in silhouette) rather than just charades. Let Clarence offer interpret for Tom.
  • make it clear that both Tom and Clarence are still learning, Tom moreso since he's interacting with the world in an inherently different manner from Clarence. Have Clarence struggle to try and explain some concepts to Tom.

That said, I'm still uncertain about what Tom himself. Is he inherently human, just from another dimension? Does he have humanlike capacity for intelligence and communication and emotion? Is he inherently similar to Clarence in age and maturity?

item.title: There’s Some Fridge Horror Here
item.content:encoded:
Obviously I love the baby boy myself as well, but honestly what I love most about this is that there’s actually some rather troubling implications from this interaction.

The whole concept hinges on the idea that the first article written by the previous researcher was laughably inaccurate at describing the complexity of the creatures mentality and threat. It was because of this bad documentation that the thing was chucked into a box for ages and allowed to suffer for no reason. I would go so far as to say that the whole “attacks and consumes all creatures it encounters” is a straight up farce. It probably just hunted and killed things occasionally because despite not requiring sustenance it still seems to experience hunger and it just didn’t know any better than to attack humans. It had the mentality of a toddler after all. The whole first article is a very clever way at poking fun at the melodrama and boring simplicity of the generic murder monster trope on the site, but in universe the generic murder monster that must be kept in a box trope is presented here as a real problem within the foundation of researchers not taking the time to fully understand an anomaly beyond its base threats or to consider the well-being of said anomaly.

This begs the question: Just how many inaccurately recorded and unreasonably contained SCPS are there?? How many generic murder monsters on this site are actually products of a biased researcher making snap judgements about complex creatures? There could be any number of sentient beings harbored by the foundation that, with proper treatment, could also learn to become more than a monster in a cage. If an article as incredibly misleading as the one Huxtable contested could go uncontested for a whole decade, it makes you wonder if maybe there are a few other articles leaving out a few key details…

I overall like the concept because it executes it in a way that feels real. There are so many points where this could have gotten cringy cutesie or forced, but it very well balanced the idea of there being an alien and possibly dangerous monster who displays a capacity to learn and has an actual personality. It’s wholesome but not overly indulgent in that fact. So yeah, it makes me feel good reading it. I also just like the idea that this Huxtable guy is part of some kind of containment reform movement that’s gonna uncover a bunch of dumb things the foundation has done over the years. Judging from this article, they sorely need one.

Anyways, TLDR: Very clever way of turning the tropes we’re used to on its head. Could have been a bit more conflict but honestly I’m just glad this thing exists. +1

item.title: Admin is Asleep, Post Antimemes (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Page Layout: Standard entry

Elevator Pitch: A rumor spreads through D Class personnel of something infiltrating the Foundation to observe the researchers, containment officers, et cetera. Originally overheard on 06/05/2020, research and containment separate and isolate the D Class personnel and wipe their memories, yet strangely, the rumor returns in each separate group of D Class in merely a week.

Central Narrative: Dr. J. Holloway is intrigued regarding the "impossible rumor" D Class has subscribed to, and turns to interviews with the personnel. They discover each individual group of D Class as a different name for the SCP, one group calling it "the Watchman," another being "the Scribe," and so on. Yet within these tight groups, there have been sightings of the illusive creature, describing it as an elongated humanoid with its legs sharpening to a single tip, its torso gaping to the point of being able to watch its lungs breathe, and what appears to be a briefcase in its hand filled with papers and pencils.

+ show block
– hide block

Although skeptical, Holloway sets the notes aside and, after obtaining permission from the lead officer in containment alongside approval from the head of research, Holloway spends the night in one of the D Class groups. Approximately halfway through the night, Holloway awakens to the sound of rustling papers and the scratches of graphite. They arise from their bed and see the creature, whom they dub "Admin," watching and presumably writing about Holloway. Holloway attempts to communicate with the creature, but to no avail, yet it seems curious over the tone of voice Holloway is using.

Further testing reveals the Admin is quite curious and has an overarching desire to learn the unlearnable. It cannot verbally communicate, but it writes quite well and is an avid enjoyer of learning how living things work.

After the incident, Holloway sends in a formal request to get the creature SCP status. While awaiting approval, they hear of sightings of the creature, sitting and watching the personnel as they rest. While Holloway never directly spoke of the creature, they have chatted with them post Admin sighting. Holloway draws the conclusion that merely speaking with someone who has directly seen the creature was enough to spread it, like a virus.

Through collaboration with the Site Director, cognitohazards with antimemetic properties are set around the site to prevent the "spread" of the SCP, along with limiting Site 23 to no other Keter class SCPs in the event of a containment breach and isolating it from the rest of the Foundation.

some of the more personal questions about his and the bars history he starts getting more dismissive and less talkative. Multiple odd things found in the bar hint to some
sort of hidden past of the place.

item.title: Re: It's An Anomalous World
item.content:encoded:
Hart Island. An uninhabited island near NYC that's been home to a barracks, a POW camp, a mental asylum, a sanitarium, a homeless shelter, a reformatory school, a rehab center, and a prison, now used as a mass grave for unclaimed and unidentified remains, miscarriages, and stillbirths. The burials here are carried out by inmates, and the bodies are frequently mixed up and put in the wrong plots. Past a certain point, no more records exist of who's buried where. It's borderline impossible to visit, since it's still part of the Department of Corrections, and the waters around it are treacherous and full of rocks. Nothing inherently anomalous about any of that, but the negative energy around this place must be insane.

item.title: Re: Zombies with cool things for hands (Seeking Greenlight)
item.content:encoded:
Made a reply, and then noticed you had edited your answer :D

Anyways, main plotline is the MTF team through the city, fighting the zombies. As they progress (about 75% in through the story), they find the kid who is crying and apologizing profusely. He tells them he just wanted something fun to happen, that everything in the town was dumb and boring, every day was just the same.

The kid is escorted to the end by the team, to show them where his house is, and the notebook. The final fight ensues, with The Final Countdown playing in the background from a zombie standing nearby with a boombox held high.

The MTF calls in helicopters to help deal with it, explosions, rock music and gunfire. As it dies, a few other kids run out from where they had been hiding while the MTF goes down in the basement to disrupt the ritual the kid started, ending the phenomena. The kids are standing in the street shouting in excitement about how awesome it was, applauding the boy who started it.

As the MTF call in help to have the mess cleaned up they hear some of the kids shouting about how it was so awesome that they should do it every week.
